opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the central limitation is that the models are *closed*. Autumn synthesizes a program that explains one particular world, a little grid-world with objects, events, and latent state that changes over time. That's genuinely impressive, because you're inferring hidden causal mechanisms just from watching. But the program you get is a self-contained, bespoke theory of that one environment. It doesn't really know that it's part of a bigger picture.

When a person figures out how some new game or gadget works, they aren't starting from scratch. They bring a huge library of concepts: gravity-like things, containers, agents with goals, switches, counters. They reuse those pieces and extend them. In Autumn, the language gives you a fixed set of primitives that we, the designers, chose. The synthesizer composes them cleverly, but it doesn't accumulate abstractions across worlds. It doesn't learn new concepts that make the next world easier to understand. So there's no real growth of knowledge, and I'd argue that growth is the essence of how science and human learning actually work.

Closely related is that the models live inside a very particular representational box. They're discrete, they're on a grid, and the dynamics are largely deterministic or have fairly simple stochasticity. The real world is continuous, noisy, partially observed at many scales, and full of things that don't decompose neatly into objects with crisp update rules. So there's a gap between "we can infer the causal program behind this toy world" and "we can build models of messy real systems that a scientist would care about."

The last piece is the cost of inference. Searching over programs is hard. We rely on fairly clever, somewhat hand-crafted heuristics for things like detecting when latent state must exist. That works in the domains we've built, but it doesn't obviously scale.

So, to sum up: the models are causal, interpretable, and executable, which is what we wanted. But they're isolated theories in a fixed language, rather than pieces of an open-ended, growing body of knowledge. Getting from the first thing to the second is, to me, the real research problem.

r001.rationale: It says Autumn does not accumulate abstractions across worlds or learn concepts that make later worlds easier to understand.

r002.rationale: It describes humans reusing concepts, but does not state that human thinking requires models that leave out parts of reality.

r003.rationale: It identifies broader research challenges, but does not pose the specific open problem of inferring which parts of reality to omit for practical usefulness.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the central limitation is that the models Autumn infers are essentially deterministic. It will find a program that explains the trace of observations you give it, and the program has these latent variables and these dynamics, but there's no real notion of uncertainty baked into the dynamics themselves. In the real world, and honestly in a lot of the games and environments we care about, things are stochastic. An object might move left or right with some probability. Autumn right now has a hard time with that, because it's looking for a deterministic explanation and it will contort itself to find one, or it will just fail.

The second thing, which is related, is that Autumn operates in a very abstracted representation. We hand it objects and cells on a grid. It's not looking at pixels, it's not doing the perception problem. So there's this whole layer between raw sensory input and the symbolic space Autumn lives in that we've basically just assumed away. If you want the full story of how an agent goes from seeing the world to inferring a causal model of it, that gap has to be filled, and we haven't filled it.

And then I'd add that the models are kind of brittle in their generality. Autumn finds a program that's consistent with the data it has seen, but there might be many programs consistent with that data, and the one it picks isn't necessarily the one that generalizes to the situations you haven't seen yet. We do some things to bias toward simpler programs, but it's not really reasoning about which hypotheses would be distinguished by future experience, which is what you'd want an agent that's actively exploring to be doing.

r001.rationale: The response says Autumn uses an abstracted representation of objects and grid cells; it identifies the missing perception layer, not an absence of abstraction.

r002.rationale: It does not state that human thinking requires models that omit parts of reality.

r003.rationale: It raises the gap between raw sensory input and symbolic models, but does not pose the problem of inferring which omissions make a model practically useful.

astra-6.text: I think the central limitation is that the observations don’t uniquely determine the model. You can infer a model that explains everything you’ve seen, but that doesn’t mean you’ve recovered the underlying mechanism. Several different rules might produce the same observed behavior and then diverge in a new situation. So the model is a hypothesis about how the system works, constrained by the observations and by the kinds of programs Autumn can express. To distinguish those hypotheses, you need further observations—or, ideally, interventions.

r001.rationale: The response describes underdetermination and limits on the programs Autumn can express, but does not identify a lack of abstraction as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It does not state that human thinking requires models that omit parts of reality.

r003.rationale: It suggests gathering observations or interventions to distinguish hypotheses, but does not pose the problem of inferring models that omit the right parts of reality for practical use.

sol-6.1.text: I think the central limitation is that a model can explain what you’ve observed without capturing the mechanism that actually generated it. There may be many programs consistent with the same sequence of observations, and those programs can make very different predictions when you intervene or encounter a new situation. So fitting the observations isn’t enough—you need some way to distinguish those competing explanations, ideally through interaction and experiment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses missing generative mechanisms and competing explanations, but does not identify absence of abstraction as the limitation.
